newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sees wheat sales from Iraq oil deal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sees wheat sales from Iraq oil deal.

text.p: Australia expected to pick up significant wheat sales to Iraq as a result of the resumption of that country's oil-for-food arrangements --- but not until early in the new year and not in "wheat bonanza" proportions.
"We would be cautiously optimistic that we could see wheat sales begin again early in the new year," Alec Nichol of the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) told Reuters.
Oil would not start to flow until around mid-December and Iraq was yet to put its wheat buying programme in place, he said. It was far too early to talk specifics, he said.

Iraq is one of Australia's most important traditional markets for wheat, regularly taking up to one million tonnes a year before the Gulf War. Since then Australia has shipped only small tonnages to the country.

Before suspension of Iraq's oil-for-food deal this September after a U.S. missile attack on the country, Australia hoped to be able to begin shipping wheat to Iraq in the third quarter of 1996 at about 100,000 tonnes a month.
This would have represented sales worth an annual US$200 million in Australian wheat exports.

The AWB had no clear view on whether it would take most of the resumed Iraq wheat market, but Australia previously held a letter of intent from Iraq indicating it as the preferred wheat supplier, Nichol said.
The U.S. at present had a very tight wheat supply situation and whether it would be able to supply any old crop wheat to Iraq might be a moot point, he said.
But Australia had an extraordinarily tight shipping schedule, having shipped 1.7 million tonnes in October and November, its biggest start to a shipping season since 1989, Nichol said.
Iraq was allowed to pump only US$2 billion worth of oil every six months and would not have access to all of that because of war reparations and other imposts, he said.
Asked about industry views that the AWB was sold out of wheat for December, Nichol said the board would continue selling if it could.
Meanwhile, on Pakistan's tender for 250,000 tonnes of wheat, expected to go mostly to Australia and the U.S., Nichol said: "The deal is not yet done".
